title: Bangladesh sets garment minimum wage at Tk 17,000; workers block highways demanding Tk 30,000
dek: The wage board's 36% rise, due from 1 December, fell well short of workers' demands. Police fired tear gas in Gazipur and 87 factories were shut on Wednesday.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Bangladesh's Minimum Wage Board has set a new minimum monthly wage of Tk 17,000 for garment workers, up from Tk 12,500, but the decision set off a fresh wave of protests on Wednesday, with workers blocking highways outside Dhaka, police firing tear gas and 87 factories shut. Workers' groups are demanding Tk 30,000.

The board agreed the figure after lengthy discussions late on Tuesday, reports said. The rise, of Tk 4,500 or 36%, must be approved by the Ministry of Labour and Employment, and the new wage structure is due to take effect on 1 December. The owners had proposed Tk 15,700 earlier on Tuesday, while the workers' representative had opened at Tk 32,000.

## Wednesday's protests

From about 8.30 am Dhaka time (8 am IST), workers blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway at Naojor in Gazipur and the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway at several points, including Sataish and Chhoydana, reports said. Traffic on the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway was halted in the Sataish area from 9 am, according to a traffic police officer, and several vehicles were damaged. About 1,000 to 1,200 workers blocked Joydebpur road and damaged the gate of a factory there.

Police fired tear gas and sound grenades to disperse crowds. Two police personnel were injured by brickbats in the Salna area and four members of the auxiliary Ansar force were also hurt, an additional police commissioner of the Gazipur Metropolitan Police said, according to reports. In Sreepur, more than 100 workers carrying sticks forced their way into four factories and damaged an administrative building, witnesses and a factory official said; several factories put up notices announcing three-day closures.

The industrial police said 35 factories stayed closed in Gazipur and 20 more declared a general holiday, while in Savar and Ashulia 32 factories were closed and workers at 10 others stopped work, reports said. Some of the Ashulia factories were shut under section 13(1) of the Bangladesh Labour Act, which lets owners close a unit without pay when workers stop work illegally.

"It is difficult to support a family on Tk 12,500 when prices keep rising," one protester in Naojor said, according to reports, adding that protests would continue until wages were raised further. Not every worker joined in: a worker in Sataish told reporters she earned about Tk 20,000 a month and that her pay had now gone up further.

## How the board got there

On Monday the owners made a first offer above Tk 14,500, which the workers' side rejected. "The factory owners' offer is too low, while they accuse us of making excessive demands," Babul Akhter, the workers' representative on the board, said then, according to reports. The owners' representative, ABM Shamsuddin, called the workers' demands unrealistic and compared the industry to "a sick duck" that cannot be expected to lay a golden egg every day. The manufacturers' association BGMEA has estimated that the protests have cost the industry $428 million and that orders worth $254 million have moved to other countries; those figures come from the employers and have not been independently checked.

On Tuesday the board's chairman, Judge Syed Azad Subhani, disclosed the owners' figure of Tk 15,700. The workers' side was reported to have lowered its demand to Tk 25,000 during the talks, although the board did not confirm that.

## How we got here

The government reconstituted the wage board on 1 November amid protests that began in October. At its first meeting on 4 November the board agreed the new wage would take effect in December, and many workers went back to work. The workers' side then formally proposed Tk 32,000 for the main grade. When a meeting due on 16 November was postponed, unrest flared again in Gazipur, Savar, Ashulia and Narayanganj, with workers blocking the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway, police using tear gas and sound grenades, and dozens of factories declaring holidays.

The gap is wide by past standards. In 2023, workers asked for about Tk 20,000 to 23,000 and settled for Tk 12,500 after the owners raised their first offer of Tk 10,400; four workers died in the protests that year, according to reports. In each of the past five wage boards, employers have opened at half or less of the workers' demand, one report said.

## Why it matters for India

Bangladesh is the world's second-largest garment exporter after China, and garments bring in about four-fifths of its export earnings, roughly $38 billion a year. Indian textile and apparel exporters compete with Bangladeshi factories for many of the same European and American buyers, so the outcome of the dispute affects costs and orders on both sides of the border. Bengal, which shares more than 2,000 km of the border, also trades heavily with Bangladesh through land ports such as Petrapole.

The dispute also lands at a fragile moment in Dhaka, where the government has deployed Border Guard Bangladesh platoons in the capital and several districts amid political violence ahead of Sheikh Hasina's planned return. Unions have threatened wider protests if the final figure falls well short of their demand.

## What happens next

The labour ministry is expected to issue the formal notice for the new wage before 1 December. Unions have said protests will go on unless the figure is raised, while owners say the industry cannot afford more. Indian exporters and the Bengal border trade will be watching whether factories reopen fully before the new rate takes effect.
